UGREEN DXP6800 Ultra and DXP8800 Ultra for TrueNAS and Unraid | ComputingForGeeks 
 Skip to content 
 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 The UGREEN DXP6800 Ultra and DXP8800 Ultra boot TrueNAS and Unraid through the same BIOS path as the older DXP boxes, but none of the community drivers that make a third-party OS comfortable on UGREEN hardware list either Ultra model as tested yet. The fan driver, the front-panel LED controller and every published hands-on review stop at the DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 172916 
 That matters because the Ultra costs $350 more than the DXP6800 Pro and $410 more than the DXP8800 Plus on Amazon, and the main hardware gains are a newer Raptor Lake U-series CPU and a 96GB memory ceiling in place of 64GB. This guide sorts what carries over to TrueNAS and Unraid, what is still unproven, and when the Ultra is the right box to buy for a ZFS or Unraid build. Prices were read from the Amazon product API on October 5, 2026, and specs come from the UGREEN spec tables and Intel ARK.
 Verdict: which DXP to buy for TrueNAS or Unraid
 For a third-party OS today, the DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus are the safer purchase. They share the Ultra layout (dual 10GbE, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two M.2 slots, one PCIe x4 slot) and have more than two years of community fan and LED work behind them. The Ultra earns its premium only for a build that will genuinely use more than 64GB of RAM, which in the 2026 memory market is an expensive plan in its own right.
 Buyer Buy Reason 
 TrueNAS or Unraid, 6 bays, under 64GB RAM DXP6800 Pro ($1,099.99) Same layout, $350 cheaper, partial fan driver support already 
 TrueNAS or Unraid, 8 bays, under 64GB RAM DXP8800 Plus ($1,369.99) LED controller lists it as tested, fan driver lists the DXP8800 
 ZFS with a large ARC or many VMs, 6 bays DXP6800 Ultra ($1,449.99) 96GB memory ceiling, Core 5 120U 
 ZFS with a large ARC or many VMs, 8 bays DXP8800 Ultra ($1,779.99) 96GB ceiling, Core 7 150U with 96 EU graphics 
 Staying on UGOS Pro Any of the four The third-party gaps below do not apply 
 DXP Ultra vs Pro and Plus: what actually changed
 UGREEN kept the chassis, the bay count and the port layout, and swapped the platform. Both Ultra CPUs are 10-core, 12-thread Raptor Lake U parts with 2 performance and 8 efficient cores, a 15 W base power and a 55 W turbo limit, according to the Intel ARK entry for the Core 5 120U and its Core 7 150U sibling. The older boxes use the 12th-gen Core i5-1235U with the same core split.
 Spec DXP6800 Ultra DXP6800 Pro DXP8800 Ultra DXP8800 Plus 
 CPU Core 5 120U Core i5-1235U Core 7 150U Core i5-1235U 
 Max turbo 5.0 GHz 4.4 GHz 5.4 GHz 4.4 GHz 
 iGPU execution units 80 80 96 80 
 RAM shipped / max 8GB DDR5 / 96GB 8GB DDR5 / 64GB 8GB DDR5 / 96GB 8GB DDR5 / 64GB 
 SATA bays + M.2 6 + 2 6 + 2 8 + 2 8 + 2 
 Network 2x 10GbE 2x 10GbE 2x 10GbE 2x 10GbE 
 Thunderbolt 4 2 2 2 2 
 PCIe slot Gen4 x4 x4, generation not stated Gen4 x4 x4, generation not stated 
 Fans 2x 90mm 2x 90mm (ITPro) 2x 120mm dual fans, size not stated 
 UGREEN power figure, drives active / hibernated 43.07 W / 24.91 W 43.07 W / 24.91 W 70.39 W / 28.99 W 70.39 W / 28.99 W 
 Amazon price, Oct 5 2026 $1,449.99 $1,099.99 $1,779.99 $1,369.99 
 The CPU change is small in practice. PassMark averages quoted by NASCompares put the Core 5 120U at 15,363 and the Core 7 150U at 14,766, so the 8-bay model is not faster on multithreaded work despite the higher turbo clock. The How-To Geek hands-on review of the DXP6800 Ultra scored it 8 out of 10 and called it only a marginal improvement over the DXP6800 Pro. That review ran UGOS Pro, not a third-party OS.
 Neither CPU supports ECC memory, and Intel ARK lists that as a flat No for both. The ODECC entry on the UGREEN spec table refers to the on-die error correction inside every DDR5 chip, which does not report corrected errors to the operating system. A ZFS build that requires end-to-end ECC does not belong on any DXP model.
 What carries over from the older DXP boxes
 The install path for the DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus is well documented, and nothing in the Ultra spec suggests a different firmware layout. NASCompares documents the procedure for Unraid on UGREEN DXP models, and the same three BIOS steps apply to a TrueNAS install:
 Connect HDMI and a USB keyboard, power on, and press Ctrl+F12 repeatedly to enter the BIOS (some units respond to F12 or Delete instead).
 Disable the watchdog timer under Advanced (on the i5 models it sat on a separate tab). Left enabled, it reboots the box every few minutes because UGOS Pro never checks in.
 Set the USB installer first in the boot order. Optionally disable the internal SSD slot to keep UGOS Pro intact and out of the way.
 UGREEN has stated that a third-party OS does not by itself change the hardware warranty, while it does not support software problems caused by that OS. Damage from disabled fans or overheating is a separate matter, which is the practical reason fan control is the first thing to sort out after the install.
 The 10GbE, SATA and NVMe controllers on the older models work with stock TrueNAS and Unraid kernels, according to community reports collected by Need to Know IT. UGREEN does not name the Ultra network or SATA controller chips on its spec pages, so treat driver support on the Ultra as likely but unconfirmed until the first lspci dumps appear.
 What is still unproven on the Ultra
 Three pieces of the third-party experience depend on reverse-engineered, model-specific work, and none of them covers the Ultra yet:
 Fan control. The UGREEN DXP fan driver project patches the it87 Super I/O driver per model. It lists the DXP2800, DXP4800 and DXP8800 as supported, the DXP6800 Pro as partial, and has no entry for either Ultra. Without it, the fans follow the BIOS curve, which a TrueNAS fan-control project for the DXP4800 describes as following CPU temperature only, not drive temperature.
 Front-panel LEDs. The ugreen_leds_controller project drives the LEDs over I2C and lists the DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus as tested. The Ultra models are missing. Under a non-UGOS system, DXP front LEDs blink in a rolling sequence by default, so a failed-disk LED is not available.
 Independent third-party OS testing. Prospective buyers have opened Unraid forum threads asking whether Unraid runs on the DXP8800 Ultra, and no published review that could be found has run TrueNAS or Unraid on either Ultra yet.
 None of this blocks a working NAS. Storage, networking and Docker apps do not depend on the LED or fan drivers. The gap is comfort and monitoring: louder or warmer than needed, and no per-bay status lights.
 TrueNAS on the DXP Ultra: RAM, ARC and the boot drive
 ZFS uses spare RAM as its ARC read cache, so the 96GB ceiling is the strongest technical reason to pick the Ultra for TrueNAS. The catch is the price of filling it. On October 5, 2026, a Crucial 32GB DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM kit (2 x 16GB) listed at $589.99, the Crucial 96GB kit was out of stock, and the cheapest in-stock 2 x 48GB SO-DIMM kit in an Amazon search was $1,614.99. Maxing the memory now costs more than the 6-bay DXP6800 Ultra itself, and close to the price of the 8-bay. For a pool of six or eight hard drives serving files and a few containers, 32GB is a sensible target, and the 64GB ceiling of the older boxes is not the limit.
 The internal 128GB SSD can serve as the TrueNAS boot device. TrueNAS recommends an SSD boot device and advises against USB sticks, so installing onto the internal SSD keeps both M.2 slots free. That install erases UGOS Pro from the SSD. Those two slots then fit a mirrored apps pool, or a mirrored special vdev for metadata. A special vdev needs at least the redundancy of the data vdevs, because losing it makes the whole pool unreadable.
 A six-bay RAIDZ2 pool keeps four drives of usable capacity and survives two failures. With 12TB WD Red Plus drives at $459.99 each, six drives cost $2,759.94 for about 48TB before ZFS overhead. The eight-bay model with RAIDZ2 keeps six drives of usable capacity. The TrueNAS vs Unraid lab test compares how each OS handles capacity, expansion and bit-rot repair on identical hardware.
 Unraid on the DXP Ultra: the license tier trap
 Unraid sells three perpetual licenses: Starter at $49 for up to 6 storage devices, Unleashed at $109 with no limit, and Lifetime at $249, which adds lifetime updates. Starter and Unleashed include one year of updates, then an optional $36 annual extension. The device count is where the DXP6800 Ultra catches buyers out.
 The Unraid licensing FAQ counts all storage devices present before array start, except one eMMC device and one USB device. Six SATA drives plus the internal 128GB UGREEN SSD makes seven devices, which is over the Starter limit before any NVMe drive goes in. Booting Unraid from that SSD does not help, because the internal boot FAQ counts an internal boot drive toward the limit too. Either disable the internal SSD slot in the BIOS, remove the SSD, or budget for Unleashed.
 Configuration Devices counted Minimum license 
 DXP6800 Ultra, 6 HDDs, internal SSD disabled 6 Starter ($49) 
 DXP6800 Ultra, 6 HDDs, internal SSD left in 7 Unleashed ($109) 
 DXP6800 Ultra, 6 HDDs + 2 NVMe cache 8 or 9 Unleashed ($109) 
 DXP8800 Ultra, any full build 8 or more Unleashed ($109) 
 The Unraid community has a fan control plugin and an LED plugin for supported UGREEN models, which is one more reason the DXP8800 Plus is the lower-friction Unraid box until those plugins add the Ultra.
 Quick Sync for Plex and Jellyfin
 Both Ultra CPUs hardware-encode and decode H.264 and HEVC through Quick Sync, and decode AV1 without encoding it. The Core 7 150U has 96 execution units against 80 on the Core 5 120U. Under TrueNAS, the Plex and Jellyfin apps have a setting that passes the Intel iGPU into the container. Under Unraid, the same works by mapping /dev/dri into the Docker container. For a household of transcoding clients, either Ultra or either older model has more than enough. The guide to the best NAS for Plex, Jellyfin and self-hosting covers how transcode capacity differs across NAS platforms.
 The DXP Ultra models and their alternatives
 UGREEN DXP6800 Ultra: six bays, 96GB ceiling
 UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Ultra, 6 bays, Core 5 120U, 2x 10GbE, 2x Thunderbolt 4. Image: UGREEN. 
 The 6-bay model at $1,449.99, the same price as on the UGREEN store . Buy it for TrueNAS with a memory plan beyond 64GB. For anything smaller, the DXP6800 Pro below runs the same OS on the same layout.
 Check price on Amazon 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Ultra: eight bays, Core 7 and bigger fans
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Ultra, 8 bays, Core 7 150U, 2x 10GbE, 2x Thunderbolt 4. Image: UGREEN. 
 The 8-bay model at $1,779.99 on Amazon and on the UGREEN store . Its two 120mm fans move more air over eight spinning drives than the 90mm pair in the 6-bay Ultra chassis. It is the Ultra to pick for an eight-wide RAIDZ2 pool with room for VMs.
 Check price on Amazon 
 Cheaper alternatives with community support
 The UGREEN DXP6800 Pro at $1,099.99 and the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus at $1,369.99 are the boxes the TrueNAS and Unraid community has actually tested. The ZimaCube 2 vs UGREEN DXP6800 comparison collects the power, noise and 10GbE throughput figures that independent reviewers measured on the DXP6800 Pro. Buyers still deciding between a prebuilt and a self-built box can check the DIY TrueNAS and Unraid builds on a mini PC , which start far below either UGREEN.
 For drives, the 16TB WD Red Pro at $699.50 and the 12TB WD Red Plus are both CMR. The NAS hard drive guide covers price per terabyte across the current lineup, and the UPS guide for a NAS covers clean shutdowns, which ZFS and the Unraid parity array both depend on.
 First-hour checks after installing TrueNAS or Unraid
 Before copying data onto an Ultra running a third-party OS, confirm the hardware the spec pages do not name. Start with the network and storage controllers:
 lspci -nn | grep -iE ' ethernet|sata|non-volatile ' 
 Both 10GbE ports and the SATA controller should appear, plus one non-volatile memory line for the 128GB system SSD and one for each populated M.2 slot. Next, check whether the Super I/O chip exposes fan readings to the stock driver:
 sudo modprobe it87 && sensors 
 No fan RPM lines, or a modprobe error, means the stock it87 driver is not exposing the fans, and they stay on the BIOS curve. TrueNAS may not ship the sensors tool at all, in which case the fan driver project above is the route. Watch drive temperatures through the first full scrub or parity check, since that is the sustained load the BIOS curve was not tuned for:
 sudo smartctl -A /dev/sda | grep -i temperature 
 Drives that settle above the high 40s Celsius during a scrub on a BIOS fan curve are the signal to set a higher fixed fan speed in the BIOS until a model-specific driver lands. Posting the lspci and sensors output to the fan driver issue tracker is also how the Ultra models get added to it.

Best NAS for Home Servers in 2026 | selfhosting.sh 
 Quick Recommendation
 For most self-hosters, buy a Synology DS425+. At $520–595 (diskless, depending on retailer), it runs Docker natively via Container Manager, has Intel Quick Sync for Plex transcoding, supports NVMe caching, and Synology’s DSM software is the most polished NAS OS on the market. Pair it with two 8 TB Seagate IronWolf drives ( $160 each) in SHR (Synology Hybrid RAID) for 8 TB usable, fault-tolerant storage at about $840–915 total.
 Want 2.5 GbE built in? The newer Synology DS925+ (~$620, AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B, 4 GB ECC RAM expandable to 32 GB) adds dual 2.5 GbE ports. It can’t hardware-transcode video like the Intel-based DS423+, but the quad-core/8-thread V1500B is roughly 47% faster in multi-threaded tasks than the DS923+‘s dual-core R1600 — a meaningful upgrade for Docker-heavy setups. Note: the DS925+ drops the PCIe expansion slot, so 10 GbE is no longer an option on this model.
 If you want maximum control and flexibility , build a DIY NAS with TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid. You’ll get more hardware for your money, but you’ll spend more time configuring it. See our DIY NAS Build Guide .
 Get the Docker Compose configs, hardware picks, and setup shortcuts we don’t put in articles. Weekly. No spam.
 What to Look For
 Drive Bays
 More bays = more storage and better redundancy options. Here’s the practical breakdown:
 2-bay: 4–36 TB usable (with RAID 1 / SHR-1). Good for getting started. Limited expansion.
 4-bay: 8–72 TB usable (with RAID 5 / SHR-1). The sweet spot for most home users. Lose one drive without data loss.
 6+ bay: For serious storage needs. Supports RAID 6 / SHR-2 (survive two simultaneous drive failures).
 Our recommendation: Start with 4 bays. You can fill two now and add two later.
 CPU
 The CPU determines whether your NAS can run Docker containers, transcode video, and handle encryption without slowing to a crawl.
 Intel (with Quick Sync): Required for Plex/Jellyfin hardware transcoding. Synology DS423+ and DS224+ both have Intel CPUs with Quick Sync.
 AMD: Better raw compute per watt, but no hardware transcoding. Synology DS923+ uses AMD Ryzen — great for everything except Plex transcoding.
 ARM: Cheap Synology models (DS120j, DS220j) use ARM chips. Avoid these for self-hosting — too slow for Docker containers and zero transcoding support.
 RAM
 2 GB: Barely enough for the NAS OS. Don’t run Docker on this.
 4 GB: Minimum for light Docker use (Pi-hole, a few small containers).
 8+ GB: Recommended. Lets you run a full Docker stack comfortably. Synology models are upgradeable — buy the base config and add RAM yourself for half the cost.
 Networking
 1 GbE: Standard. Fine for streaming and normal file access. Bottleneck for large file transfers.
 2.5 GbE: The new standard. Synology DS925+ has it built in. Otherwise, add it via USB adapter.
 10 GbE: Overkill for most homes. Matters for video editing or multi-user environments. Available via PCIe expansion on DS923+ and DS1621+.
 Docker Support
 Not all NAS devices support Docker. Synology runs Docker via Container Manager (formerly Docker package). QNAP runs Docker via Container Station. TrueNAS SCALE runs Docker natively on Linux. TrueNAS CORE (FreeBSD) does NOT run Docker — it uses jails.
 Top Picks
 1. Synology DS425+ — Best Overall
 The DS425+ is the successor to the DS423+. It’s a 4-bay NAS with an Intel Celeron processor and hardware Quick Sync for Plex/Jellyfin transcoding. Synology’s DSM software handles Docker containers, file sharing, and backups through a polished web UI. It supports both 2.5” and 3.5” drives and can handle up to 80 TB of raw storage.

 Note: Unlike the DS425+, the DS224+ does not have NVMe cache slots. If you need SSD caching for better random I/O, choose the DS425+ or DS925+.
 Best for: Entry-level NAS users. Pair with two 8 TB IronWolf drives (~$160 each) for a ~$690 total setup.
 4. DIY NAS with TrueNAS SCALE — Best for Maximum Control
 Build your own using a Jonsbo N3 case (8 bays), an Intel N305 motherboard, and 32 GB DDR5. Run TrueNAS SCALE for ZFS with native Docker support.
 Spec Detail

 Pros: 
 More storage capacity than any pre-built under $1,000
 ZFS — the gold standard for data integrity
 Full Docker/Kubernetes support on TrueNAS SCALE
 No vendor lock-in
 8 cores for heavy container workloads
 Cons: 
 You build and maintain it yourself
 TrueNAS has a steeper learning curve than DSM
 No mobile app ecosystem like Synology Drive/Photos
 No hardware warranty on the complete system
 Best for: Experienced users who want ZFS, maximum storage density, and full control. See our DIY NAS Build Guide for step-by-step instructions.
 5. Unraid on Any x86 Hardware — Best Flexibility
 Unraid isn’t hardware — it’s an OS. Install it on any x86 PC (old desktop, mini PC, server). Its killer feature: mix any size drives in a single array. Add a 4 TB today, an 8 TB tomorrow, a 16 TB next month. No rebuilding, no matching.

 Excellent Docker and VM support

 What Can You Run on a NAS?
 Every NAS (2+ GB RAM):
 File sharing (SMB, NFS, AFP)
 Automated backups (Hyper Backup, rsync, Borg)

 Plex or Jellyfin — media server (Intel CPU recommended for transcoding)

 8+ GB RAM NAS:
 Everything above, plus:
 Home Assistant — home automation
 BookStack — wiki/knowledge base
 Uptime Kuma — monitoring
 Multiple databases (PostgreSQL, MariaDB)
 16+ GB RAM (DIY/Unraid):
 Everything above, plus:
 Virtual machines

 Large Nextcloud instances with full-text search
 FAQ
 Should I buy a Synology or build my own?
 Buy a Synology if you value your time and want everything to “just work.” Build your own if you want maximum storage per dollar, ZFS, or specific hardware requirements. The DS425+ at ~$520–595 is hard to beat for convenience. A DIY 8-bay build costs $400–600 (without drives) but gives you twice the capacity and more powerful hardware.
 How many drives should I start with?
 Start with two drives in a 4-bay NAS. Use SHR/RAID 1 for redundancy (you get one drive’s worth of usable space). Add more drives as you need them. Starting with two 8 TB IronWolf drives gives you 8 TB usable for ~$320.
 Do I need a NAS if I have a mini PC?
 They complement each other. Use a mini PC for compute (Docker containers, VMs, transcoding) and a NAS for bulk storage (media, backups, photos). Connect them over your LAN with NFS or SMB mounts. This separation is cleaner and more reliable than trying to do everything on one device.
 Which drives should I buy?
 See our Best Hard Drives for NAS guide. Short answer: Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Plus in 8–16 TB capacities for the best price per TB.

 The DIY TrueNAS route saves $100–200 over Synology at 4 bays and significantly more at 8+ bays. But factor in your time — a Synology setup takes 20 minutes, TrueNAS takes hours the first time.

Best NAS Case (2026): Mini-ITX to 12-Bay TrueNAS Chassis | ComputingForGeeks 
 Skip to content 
 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 A NAS case comes down to two numbers: how many drives it holds, and how warm those drives run once it is full. Everything else, the aluminum finish, the walnut trim, the lockable door, is secondary to whether eight spinning disks stay under temperature during a scrub. For years the honest answer to “which case” was a used SilverStone or a Fractal Node 304, because almost nothing was built for the job. That changed. Jonsbo now sells a whole ladder of purpose-built NAS chassis, and the category finally has a real gradient from a five-bay cube up to a twelve-bay tower.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 171286 
 The eight picks below cover the three families that matter now: the compact Jonsbo boxes that pack five to twelve bays into the smallest possible footprint, the traditional steel towers that trade size for a lockable hot-swap cage and a standard power supply, and a 4U rackmount chassis for builds that live in a rack. If you would rather skip the build entirely, a prebuilt NAS is the other route. Which case fits depends on the rest of the parts list, so this pairs with the full TrueNAS build , the HBA that drives the bays once the board runs out of SATA ports, and the drives that go in them. With drive prices where they are in 2026, the bay-count math has shifted toward fewer, larger disks, which changes the case you should buy.
 Specs, bay counts, and prices verified October 2026 against manufacturer datasheets and live retail listings. 
 The short answer: the Jonsbo N3 is the best NAS case for most compact TrueNAS or Unraid builds, with eight hot-swap bays on a mini-ITX board in about 18 liters. Step up to the Jonsbo N6 for nine bays, micro-ATX, and a full ATX power supply. For twelve bays, the Jonsbo N5 is the desk-friendly tower and the Rosewill RSV-L4412U is the rackmount answer. The SilverStone CS382 is the pick when the drives must sit behind a lockable door.
 The eight NAS cases at a glance
 Every case here takes 3.5-inch drives on a hot-swap tray or backplane, though the N4 hot-swaps only four of its six. The differences that decide the purchase are the bay count, the board and power-supply size the chassis accepts, and how much room is left for a cooler and an add-in card. Prices move week to week, so treat the figures in each section as a band and confirm the live number before buying.
 Case 3.5″ bays Hot-swap Board PSU Volume Best for 
 Jonsbo N2 5 (+1x 2.5″) Yes, SATA backplane Mini-ITX SFX ~11 L Smallest first NAS 
 Jonsbo N4 6 (+2x 2.5″) 4 of 6 bays Micro-ATX SFX ~20 L Micro-ATX on a budget 
 Jonsbo N3 8 (+1x 2.5″) Yes, SATA backplane Mini-ITX SFX ~18 L Compact eight-bay default 
 SilverStone CS382 8 (+3 internal) Yes, SAS-12G/SATA Micro-ATX ATX 39.6 L Serviceable hot-swap 
 SilverStone CS380 8 (+2x 5.25″) Yes, SAS/SATA ATX ATX 44.7 L Standard-parts value 
 Jonsbo N6 9 Yes, SATA backplane Micro-ATX ATX or SFX ~34 L Nine bays, ATX power 
 Jonsbo N5 12 (+4x 2.5″) Yes, SATA backplane up to E-ATX ATX ~49 L Twelve bays on a desk 
 Rosewill RSV-L4412U 12 Yes, three 4-bay cages up to E-ATX ATX 4U, ~50 L Twelve bays in a rack 
 1. Jonsbo N2: the smallest sensible NAS
 Five bays in eleven liters is about as small as a real NAS gets before you give up drive count entirely.
 Jonsbo N2: five 3.5-inch hot-swap bays in an eleven-liter aluminum cube. Image: Jonsbo. 
 The N2 holds five 3.5-inch drives on a front SATA backplane plus one 2.5-inch SSD for the operating system, all on a mini-ITX board. That is enough for a four-wide RAIDZ1 with a hot spare, or a five-wide RAIDZ2, which suits most first builds. It is the case to buy when the goal is a quiet appliance that disappears on a shelf rather than a machine you expand for years. A genuine unit runs around $120 to $140; check the live price .
 Skip it if you expect to grow. The SFX-only power supply and the 65mm cooler ceiling force small, specific parts, and there is no staggered spin-up, so the PSU has to swallow the inrush of five drives at once. The backplane fan header also runs the stock 120mm fan at full speed unless you reroute it to a motherboard PWM header, which is the first thing to change after the build. Five bays is the hard limit here, not a starting point.
 2. Jonsbo N4: micro-ATX and walnut for the price of a cube
 The N4 is the cheapest way into a micro-ATX board in a Jonsbo box, and the walnut front is why it keeps turning up in searches for a retro NAS case.
 Jonsbo N4: six 3.5-inch bays, four of them hot-swap, under a micro-ATX board compartment. Image: Jonsbo. 
 Where the N2 and N3 stop at mini-ITX, the N4 takes a micro-ATX board in its upper compartment, which buys more SATA ports, more memory slots, and four low-profile expansion slots for an HBA and a NIC. The lower compartment holds six 3.5-inch drives, four on a hot-swap backplane and two fixed, plus two 2.5-inch SSDs. It is about 20 liters, runs an SFX power supply up to 125mm long, and cools the drives with a single 120mm fan. The white unit with the walnut panel sells for around $120 to $140; check the live price . Stock on this variant was thin in October 2026, so check before building a parts list around it.
 The micro-ATX support comes with real limits. The board compartment clears only a 70mm cooler and cards up to 230mm, all low profile, so a full-height HBA or a GPU for transcoding will not fit. Two of the six drives are not hot-swap, which matters the day one of them fails. Skip it if you want eight hot-swap bays in a similar footprint; the N3 does that on a smaller board, and the larger N6 adds a ninth bay and room for full-height cards.
 3. Jonsbo N3: the compact eight-bay default
 Eight 3.5-inch bays in eighteen liters is the sweet balance most compact DIY builds land on.
 Jonsbo N3: eight 3.5-inch hot-swap bays on an SFX-powered mini-ITX board. Image: Jonsbo. 
 The N3 puts eight hot-swap 3.5-inch bays and one 2.5-inch OS slot on a mini-ITX board, cooled by two built-in 100mm fans across the drive compartment. It fits an SFX power supply up to 105mm and a cooler up to 130mm, which is generous for the size and enough for a real air cooler rather than a low-profile part. This is the case most compact builds should default to: eight bays covers a six-wide RAIDZ2 with room to grow, in a box that still fits on a desk. Pre-owned or new, it runs about $150 to $175; check the live price .
 The catch is the SATA count. A mini-ITX board rarely has eight SATA ports, so filling the N3 usually means adding a host bus adapter or a PCIe SATA card in its single slot, which is where the HBA guide comes in. The backplane also ships without SATA cables and runs its fans at full tilt off the backplane header, so budget for a set of angled SATA cables and plan to reroute the fans. Skip it if you need the drives behind a lockable door, since the trays are open at the front.
 4. SilverStone CS382: hot-swap without giving up an ATX power supply
 This is the case for people who want front-loading hot-swap trays and a standard power supply in the same box.
 SilverStone CS382: eight hot-swap SAS or SATA bays behind a lockable door on a micro-ATX board. Image: SilverStone. 
 The CS382 fits a micro-ATX board and a full ATX power supply, and its eight front bays sit behind a lockable door on a real backplane wired for SAS-12G or SATA-6G. Two 92mm fans pull air straight across the drive cage, and there is room internally for another 3.5-inch drive, two 2.5-inch drives, and an optical bay. Cooler clearance is 168mm and cards can run to 369mm, so a proper tower cooler and a long HBA both fit. In a 39.6-liter footprint it is far easier to service than any of the compact cubes. Expect roughly $225 to $260, and it goes in and out of stock; check the live price .
 The SAS-12G backplane is not plug and play. SATA drives connect straight through, but running SAS drives or wiring all eight bays cleanly wants a SAS host bus adapter and a mini-SAS HD to SATA breakout cable, not the motherboard ports. Skip it if you wanted something small, because at over 39 liters this is a proper mini-tower, and the 174mm card-width limit rules out some triple-slot GPUs if the box ever doubles as more than a NAS.
 5. SilverStone CS380: eight hot-swap bays on standard parts
 The CS380 is the cheapest way to get eight front hot-swap bays without touching an aluminum boutique case or a SAS backplane you have to think about.
 SilverStone CS380: eight hot-swap bays and two 5.25-inch bays in a standard ATX tower. Image: SilverStone. 
 Where the CS382 is micro-ATX and modern, the CS380 is a full ATX tower that takes any standard ATX board and power supply. Its eight hot-swap 3.5-inch bays sit in two modular four-bay cages, fed by two dedicated 120mm intake fans with a third 120mm on the rear, plus two 5.25-inch bays up top for whatever a build still needs. Seven expansion slots leave plenty of room for an HBA and a NIC. It is the value option in this list: the same eight-bay hot-swap capability on the most ordinary parts you can buy, usually around $220 to $250; check the live price .
 It is the oldest design here and it shows in the clearances. Cooler height caps at 146mm and card width at 149mm, tighter than the CS382, so a big dual-tower air cooler will not fit and neither will some wide GPUs. The drives are cooled only by the two side intakes, which is adequate but not generous under a full-array scrub. Skip it if you want the smallest box or the quietest one, because at 44.7 liters it is the bigger of the two SilverStone towers and far larger than any of the compact cubes.
 6. Jonsbo N6: nine bays and a full ATX power supply
 The N6 is the newest Jonsbo NAS case and the one that fixes the most complaints about the older cubes.
 Jonsbo N6: nine 3.5-inch bays on a SATA backplane, micro-ATX, and ATX or SFX power. Image: Jonsbo. 
 Nine 3.5-inch bays sit in a lower compartment on metal trays that plug into a single SATA backplane, with two built-in 120mm fans across the drives and a three-speed fan controller on the front. The board compartment takes mini-ITX or micro-ATX with four full-height slots, and the power supply can be an ATX unit up to 220mm or an SFX unit up to 100mm. That ATX option is the headline: none of the smaller Jonsbo boxes take a standard power supply. Cooler clearance runs from 65mm to 160mm and card length from 275mm to 320mm depending on where the power supply goes. At about 34 liters it is larger than an N3 but far smaller than the N5. It sells for around $170 to $190; check the live price .
 Nine bays is an awkward number for ZFS until you use it as an eight-wide RAIDZ2 plus a hot spare, which is exactly how most N6 builds end up. The backplane breaks out to individual SATA data connectors with SATA and Molex power, so there is no SAS support and a nine-drive array needs an HBA with breakout cables. The trays have no activity LEDs, so match serial numbers before pulling one. Mounting the ATX power supply above the board cuts cooler height sharply, so pick the cooler after deciding where the PSU goes. Skip it if you need more than nine drives, because at that point the N5 or a rackmount chassis is the better box.
 7. Jonsbo N5: twelve bays and room for a card
 Twelve hot-swap 3.5-inch bays plus four 2.5-inch mounts is where a DIY NAS stops being an appliance and starts being a real storage server.
 Jonsbo N5: twelve 3.5-inch hot-swap bays plus four 2.5-inch mounts on an E-ATX board. Image: Jonsbo. 
 The N5 fronts twelve hot-swap 3.5-inch bays across two backplanes and adds four side-mounted 2.5-inch drives, on a board up to full E-ATX. It takes a standard ATX power supply and a 160mm cooler, has eight expansion slots, and clears cards to 350mm, so a full HBA and even a GPU for transcoding both fit. Twelve bays is enough for a wide RAIDZ2 or two six-wide vdevs, which is the point at which the pool layout matters more than the case. The walnut front is the marketing, the drive count is the reason to buy. It runs about $240 to $270; check the live price .
 Two things to plan for. The power supply must be 170mm or shorter to keep all twelve front bays, because a longer ATX unit forces the removal of the four-bay cage and drops you to eight. And the backplanes ship without cables and need Molex power splitters plus long SATA runs, routed before the PSU goes in, along with an HBA on most boards to reach twelve drives. Skip it if noise matters, because thin steel and twelve spinning disks make it one of the loudest cases here.
 8. Rosewill RSV-L4412U: a 12-bay NAS chassis for the rack
 When the NAS is going into a 19-inch rack rather than onto a desk, this is the 12-bay chassis that costs less than most of the enterprise alternatives.
 Rosewill RSV-L4412U: twelve hot-swap 3.5-inch bays behind a lockable bezel in a 4U chassis. Image: Rosewill. 
 The RSV-L4412U is a 4U chassis with twelve hot-swap 3.5-inch bays in three four-bay cages, each on its own small backplane that accepts SATA or SAS drives. It takes any board up to E-ATX, a standard ATX power supply up to 220mm, and seven expansion slots, which is room for an HBA, a 10GbE card, and a GPU at once. A wall of three 120mm fans sits behind the cages with two 80mm fans at the rear, and twelve SATA cables come in the box. Cooler clearance is 152mm without the GPU holder fitted. Expect around $370 to $400; check the live price .
 Check the rack before the chassis. It is 650mm deep and weighs almost 15kg empty, so it needs a full-depth rack and rails rather than a short wall-mount cabinet, which the first rackmount server guide covers. Each four-bay cage takes two Molex power leads, so count the Molex connectors on the power supply or budget for adapters. Skip it if the machine lives in a living space: the stock fans are tuned for airflow over quiet, and a 4U box is not a shelf ornament.
 Best 12-bay NAS case: tower or rackmount
 Twelve bays is where the choice splits by location, not by quality. The Jonsbo N5 and the Rosewill RSV-L4412U both hold twelve 3.5-inch drives on an E-ATX board with an ATX power supply, and both need an HBA to reach the full count on almost any motherboard.
 12-bay case Form Extra drives PSU limit for all 12 bays Slots Fits in 
 Jonsbo N5 Desktop tower, ~49 L 4x 2.5″ ATX up to 170mm 8 A desk, a shelf, a closet 
 Rosewill RSV-L4412U 4U rackmount, 650mm deep None ATX up to 220mm 7 A full-depth 19-inch rack 
 The N5 wins on looks, the 2.5-inch mounts, and the fact that it needs no rack. The Rosewill wins on serviceability, because every bay loads from the front behind a locking bezel, and on power supply choice, since it keeps all twelve bays with any ATX unit up to 220mm. Twelve large drives pull real power at spin-up, so size the UPS alongside the power supply. Past twelve bays, the next step is a used enterprise chassis or a SAS expander, not a bigger consumer case.
 Match the case to the motherboard
 The board decides the case more often than the drive count does, and it is the part most NAS builds pick first. A TrueNAS build that wants ECC memory usually lands on a micro-ATX or ATX workstation or server board, which rules out the mini-ITX cubes before bay count comes up. The ECC question is worth settling before ordering anything.
 Board size Cases that take it What it usually means 
 Mini-ITX N2, N3 (and N4, N6) One PCIe slot, often four SATA ports, an HBA fills the rest 
 Micro-ATX N4, N6, CS382 (and N5, CS380, RSV-L4412U) Two to four slots, room for an HBA plus a 10GbE NIC 
 ATX CS380, N5, RSV-L4412U Workstation and server boards with ECC and more lanes 
 E-ATX N5, RSV-L4412U Dual-socket and large server boards 
 For the best mini-ITX NAS case specifically, the N3 is the default and the N2 is the smaller fallback; both take the single slot a mini-ITX board offers. For a small build on a mini PC instead of a full board, the mini PC NAS route skips the case question almost entirely.
 Compact aluminum or traditional steel
 The real decision is which of the two families fits the build. The Jonsbo cubes win on size and looks. They put five to twelve bays in the smallest possible box, but they pay for it with an SFX power supply on the smaller models, tighter cooler clearance, and drive trays that are open at the front. The SilverStone chassis are larger and plainer, and in exchange they take a standard ATX power supply, hide the drives behind a lockable door, and are far easier to service because the whole hot-swap cage faces forward.
 If the NAS lives on a desk or a shelf and the drive count is settled, the aluminum boxes are the better buy. If it lives in a closet or a rack-adjacent spot where you will pull drives without warning and want a normal power supply, the steel SilverStone cases earn their extra size. If it lives in a rack, the Rosewill is the only pick here that belongs there. Everything else, the wood trim and the anodizing included, is aesthetics.
 One non-hot-swap option keeps coming in and out of stock: the Fractal Design Node 804, the micro-ATX cube that was the default DIY NAS case before Jonsbo arrived. It holds up to ten 3.5-inch drives on internal brackets with three fans included, and it ran about $130 to $140 the last time Amazon had it; the listing was out of stock again in October 2026. Every drive swap means opening the case, which is the trade for a quieter, more conventional build. If you want the same micro-ATX footprint today, the Jonsbo N6 above takes the same boards and an ATX power supply and adds hot-swap trays.
 Count bays for the drives you will actually buy
 Bay count used to be the whole decision. It is less so now. A single modern 3.5-inch drive holds more than an entire array did a few years ago, and with prices elevated the sensible build uses fewer, larger disks rather than filling every bay with small ones. A four-wide RAIDZ1 of large drives can carry more usable capacity than an eight-wide array of old ones, at lower power and less heat, which means a five-bay N2 covers far more builds than its size suggests.
 Buy the case for the array you will actually run, plus one bay for a future replacement, not for a theoretical maximum. The one place extra bays pay off is a wide RAIDZ2 or a two-vdev pool, where the layout of the pool sets the bay count. And whatever the count, confirm the drives are conventional recording and not shingled before they go in, because a case full of SMR disks resilvers for days regardless of how many bays it has.
 Hot-swap is convenience, not redundancy
 Every case here advertises hot-swap bays, and the feature is worth having, but it is often misread. A hot-swap tray lets you pull and replace a failed drive without powering down or opening the case. It does nothing for data safety on its own. The redundancy comes from the pool layout, a RAIDZ level or a mirror, not from the tray. A single-disk pool in a twelve-bay hot-swap case is exactly as fragile as a single disk anywhere else.
 Where hot-swap earns its keep is time to repair. When a drive fails at 3 a.m., pulling the labelled tray and sliding a new disk in beats shutting the array down and fishing a drive out of a cabled cage. That is a real operational win on a NAS that other people depend on, and it is the main reason to pay for the SilverStone door-and-cage design over an open Jonsbo tray. It is not a reason to run less redundancy in the pool.
 PSU, cooler, and HBA clearance
 Three clearances trip up more NAS builds than drive count ever does. The first is the power supply. The N2, N3, and N4 take SFX units only, which are pricier and less common than ATX, while the N6, N5, both SilverStone cases, and the Rosewill take a standard ATX supply. On the N5 the ATX unit has to be 170mm or shorter to keep all twelve bays, a limit easy to miss when buying a high-wattage PSU.
 The second is cooler height, which ranges from a cramped 65mm in the N2 to a comfortable 168mm in the CS382, so the case decides the cooler, not the other way round. The third is the add-in card. Almost every one of these builds needs a host bus adapter to reach its full drive count, so the case must have a free slot with real clearance for it, and that card runs hot in a sealed box. Confirm all three against the board and the parts list before ordering, because a case that will not close over the cooler is the most common reason a build stalls.
 Pairs with Best Synology Alternatives: UGREEN vs QNAP vs UniFi UNAS vs DIY 
 ZimaCube 2 NAS Guide: Drives, RAID, Review Data 
 Best External Hard Drives for Linux Backups 2026 
 What to watch on the drive temperatures
 The case is only doing its job if the drives stay cool under load, and a scrub or a resilver is when that gets tested. Backblaze, which runs hundreds of thousands of drives, found effectively no correlation between drive temperature and failure across its fleet, which mostly runs between 15 and 30 degrees Celsius against a manufacturer-rated ceiling near 60. The practical target for a home NAS is therefore not “as cold as possible” but “comfortably under about 40 degrees Celsius while every disk is being read at once.” A sealed aluminum cube with two small fans and a front-fan steel cage reach that differently, and the only way to know is to measure your own build.
 After the array is up, read the temperature straight from each disk with smartctl:
 sudo smartctl -A /dev/sda | grep -i temperature 
 Attribute 194, Temperature_Celsius, is the number that matters, and its raw value is the current reading. Some drives report it as attribute 190 instead, which the grep above also catches. Kick off a pool scrub, watch every drive at once, and the case has passed if the hottest disk in the middle of the stack holds inside range while the whole array is under read. If it climbs past 45 degrees, the fix is airflow before anything else: reroute the backplane fans to a motherboard header so they ramp under load, swap the stock fans for higher static-pressure ones, or in the compact cubes accept fewer, larger drives to cut the heat at the source. The bays are only as good as the air moving across them.

Best NAS for Homelab (2026): UGREEN vs TerraMaster vs Synology Skip to main content 
 This isn’t a generic “best NAS” list. Those exist, and PCMag writes them better than I can. This is for homelab people: you want a box that stores files and runs Docker containers, hosts a VM or two, feeds Plex/Jellyfin transcoding, and talks fast to your Proxmox cluster over NFS or iSCSI. That narrows the field to NAS units with real CPUs, enough RAM headroom, and 2.5GbE or better networking.
 Affiliate disclosure
 Some links on this page are affiliate links. If you buy through them, I earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.
 How I picked these
 I started with every NAS on Amazon shipping an x86 CPU, 8GB+ RAM (or an upgrade slot), at least one M.2 NVMe bay, and 2.5GbE networking, then cut anything above $1,300 diskless. ARM-only units are out (most VM images and a chunk of container images won’t run), and so are boxes with soldered, non-upgradable RAM under 8GB.
 What’s left is a short list. I evaluated each on four things: CPU performance per dollar, RAM ceiling, out-of-box networking speed, and whether the OS lets you run Docker and VMs without hacks. I also weighed the option of skipping a NAS entirely and building a mini PC + DAS; for some homelabs that’s the better call.

 What actually matters for a Docker/Proxmox NAS
 RAM headroom. Docker containers and a couple of VMs eat RAM faster than CPU. 8GB is the floor; 32GB is comfortable. Non-upgradable RAM (looking at you, soldered models) is a hard stop.
 An NVMe slot for apps. Spinning disks are for bulk storage. Container volumes, databases, and VM disks belong on the M.2 slots every pick here includes.
 2.5GbE minimum. Containers serving your LAN and Proxmox nodes pulling VM disks over NFS saturate 1GbE instantly. 10GbE future-proofs the link to your main server and the switch everything hangs off.
 x86 CPU. ARM NAS units are cheaper but rule out most VM images and some container images. Every pick below is x86.
 Transcoding. If Jellyfin/Plex lives on the NAS, you want Intel QuickSync, which the Synology’s Ryzen doesn’t have. If it doesn’t have to live on the NAS, a small Intel box handles it: see the best mini PC for Plex and Jellyfin .
 1. UGREEN DXP2800: the $340 entry point
 UGREEN DXP2800 
 $339.99 on Oct 23 (list $389.99) · 4.6★, 951 ratings · shipped by Amazon, sold by UGREEN · it was the #1 Best Seller in NAS devices when I first checked on Sep 21
 Two bays, Intel N100, 8GB DDR5, a single 2.5GbE port, and two M.2 NVMe slots. The NVMe slots matter more than the bays for this audience: put your container volumes and app databases on NVMe and let the HDDs be pure bulk storage. UGOS supports Docker and VMs, so the whole home-server container stack runs on it.
 Where it fits: a first NAS, a Plex/Jellyfin box for a small library, or a dedicated backup target for your Proxmox cluster (a cheap NAS doing one job well is a legitimate architecture). Where it doesn’t: heavy VM duty or anything needing more than ~80TB of raw capacity (two bays × 24TB NAS drives, RAID 1). Two bays also means RAID 1 or nothing, so plan your redundancy accordingly.

 UGOS (UGREEN’s OS) has Docker and VM support built in, and UGREEN officially lets you install TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox instead, with no warranty games.  3. TerraMaster F4-424 Pro: the compute king

 The i3-N305 gives you 8 cores and 8 threads (the strongest CPU here) plus 32GB of DDR5 out of the box . For Docker-heavy workloads that’s the most capable machine in this list: the RAM you actually need is already installed.
 The catch is TOS, TerraMaster’s operating system. It works (Docker support exists) but it’s the weakest software of the three, and TerraMaster had documented security issues in 2022–2023: deadbolt ransomware targeted TOS vulnerabilities, and patches were slow. The community’s fix is well-worn: buy the hardware, flash TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid , and never boot TOS. If that plan appeals to you, this is your box. If you want a turnkey appliance you’ll never SSH into, look at the Synology or UGREEN instead.

 4. Synology DS925+: the software king, with asterisks
 Synology DS925+ 
 $742.62 (list $889.99) · 4.2★, 156 reviews · Amazon’s Choice
 DSM is still the best NAS software by a mile: Active Backup, Photos, Drive, Surveillance Station, and a container manager that just works. If the point of the NAS is to be a reliable appliance you’ll forget about for five years, this is the safe pick.
 The asterisks are real, though. The Ryzen V1500B is a 4-core chip with no integrated GPU, so no hardware transcoding , which rules it out as a Jellyfin box for remote clients. It ships with 4GB of RAM you’ll want to upgrade immediately. And the DS925+ generation restricts storage to Synology’s drive compatibility list, which pushed a chunk of the community toward third-party NAS brands this year. Docker containers run fine in Container Manager; for Proxmox it’s a storage target, not a compute node.

 5. UGREEN DXP6800 Pro: the small-server replacement
 UGREEN DXP6800 Pro 
 $1,049.99 on Oct 23 (list $1,209.99) · 4.5★, 90 ratings · shipped by Amazon, sold by UGREEN
 The premium end of the range, and it earns it: a 10-core/12-thread i5-1235U, two 10GbE ports (aggregable to 20G), two Thunderbolt 4 ports for direct-attach editing, a built-in 128GB SSD for the OS, 6 SATA bays plus 2 M.2 NVMe for up to 208TB, and RAID 0/1/5/6/10. That’s the spec sheet of a small tower server, not an appliance. It can host the whole container stack plus several VMs while serving storage to a Proxmox cluster over 10GbE.
 The audience here is narrower: homelabbers consolidating into one “do-everything” box, or small offices. At $1,050 diskless, price it against a mini PC + DAS build first. The mini PC gets you more compute for less money. The 6800 Pro gets you six hot-swap bays in one box with a 3-year warranty.

 Drives are the expensive half of a NAS right now. Every new-condition hard drive listing I checked on Oct 23 was from a third-party seller, and the cheapest price per TB was a renewed enterprise drive. Three rules before the table:
 CMR only. SMR drives (plain WD Red, most desktop drives) take far longer to rebuild a RAID array or resilver a ZFS pool, and a slow rebuild is when a second drive fails. Seagate IronWolf and IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus and Red Pro, and Toshiba N300 are CMR lines.

Four of them in RAID 5 on the DXP4800 Plus give you 36TB usable for about $1,800. For container volumes and VM disks, put an NVMe drive in the M.2 slots and keep the hard drives for bulk storage.
 Also worth knowing
 UGREEN DXP480T Plus (~$999): the all-flash sibling. 4x NVMe bays, no SATA, 10GbE. If your homelab data fits in ~16TB of SSD (and you value silence over raw capacity), it’s a clean option. The lack of SATA bays means no cheap bulk storage, though. Every TB costs flash prices.
 QNAP TS-464: a year ago this was a contender. The Intel N5095 is showing its age against the N305 and Pentium Gold 8505 in the picks above, QNAP’s software has had its own security troubles, and the price hasn’t dropped to match. I’d skip it this cycle.
 Or skip the NAS: mini PC + DAS
 Before buying a NAS at all, price the alternative: an N150 mini PC running Proxmox or plain Docker, plus a USB DAS enclosure for the bulk disks. On Oct 23 that was a Beelink EQ14 at $369 (16GB, dual 2.5GbE; more options in the home server mini PC guide ) and a TerraMaster D4-320 at $170.99 (4 bays over 10Gbps USB-C, 4.2★ from 395 ratings). That’s about $540 diskless, against $657 for the DXP4800 Plus.

 If you already run a Proxmox mini PC or plan to, a NAS appliance is mostly redundant. Attach storage to the cluster and be done. Buy the NAS when you want storage to be a separate, boring, always-on appliance that survives your cluster experiments.
 One caveat with the DAS route: a USB enclosure puts a USB bridge between the disks and the OS. ZFS and mdadm work on it, but a flaky bridge shows up as disks dropping out of the pool. On day one, check that SMART data comes through ( smartctl -a /dev/sdX ) and leave the pool under load for a few hours before you trust it with data.
 If I were buying today
 Under $400: The DXP2800 . It runs Docker and VMs, the N100 sips power, and you can always add a second NAS later if you outgrow two bays.
 Best overall for homelab: The DXP4800 Plus . 10GbE at $657 is a hardware gap nobody else closes, and the 64GB RAM ceiling means you won’t hit a wall.
 Most compute for the money: The F4-424 Pro , but only if you’re flashing your own OS. The i3-N305 + 32GB out of the box is hard to beat if you never plan to touch TOS.
 Best appliance experience: The DS925+ . Accept no transcoding and the drive whitelist, and you get software that genuinely works for five years with minimal attention.
 Money no object, one box: The DXP6800 Pro . i5, dual 10GbE, six bays, TB4. It replaces a small server.
 And whichever you buy, put it on a UPS. A CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the $240 insurance that keeps a hard power cut from corrupting your array. If the NAS sits in a rack, the best rack mount UPS guide covers 1U and 2U units. More on that and the rest of the homelab stack in my Black Friday deals tracker and the Docker containers guide .
 FAQ
 What is the best NAS for a homelab in 2026? For most homelabs, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: $656.99 on Oct 23, 10GbE plus 2.5GbE, 4 bays plus 2 NVMe slots, RAM up to 64GB, and official support for running TrueNAS, Unraid or Proxmox instead of UGOS. Under $400, the DXP2800. If you want the best software and don’t need hardware transcoding, the Synology DS925+.
 Which hard drives should I put in a NAS? CMR NAS drives: Seagate IronWolf or IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus or Red Pro, Toshiba N300. Avoid SMR drives in any RAID or ZFS pool. On Oct 23 the best new-drive value I found was the Seagate IronWolf 12TB at $449.99 ($37.50 per TB) from a third-party seller. A renewed Exos X24 was cheaper per TB, with a refurbisher warranty instead of Seagate’s.
 Can these NAS units run Docker containers directly? Yes. All three support Docker natively (UGREEN and Synology have container managers in their OS; TerraMaster supports Docker in TOS). For heavier VM workloads, the UGREEN and TerraMaster hardware handles it; the Synology’s 4GB of base RAM needs an upgrade first.
 Do I need 10GbE for a homelab NAS? Not strictly. 2.5GbE saturates HDDs fine (~280MB/s). 10GbE matters when you add NVMe pools, run VM disks over NFS/iSCSI, or have multiple clients hitting the NAS at once. The DXP4800 Plus having it at $657 removes the dilemma.
 What's the Synology drive whitelist issue? The DS925+ generation only supports drives on Synology’s compatibility list, which favors Synology-branded and enterprise drives and excludes many popular WD/Seagate models. It’s the main reason long-time Synology users have been defecting to UGREEN and DIY builds.
 NAS or just a big USB drive on my mini PC? A DAS enclosure on a mini PC is cheaper and simpler for single-server setups. Buy the NAS when you want RAID management, snapshots, and backups handled by software designed for it, or when storage needs to stay up while your compute boxes get experimented on.
 How much RAM do I need for Docker on a NAS? 8GB runs a handful of containers. If you’re adding Immich, a Plex instance, a couple of databases, and maybe a Home Assistant VM, 32GB is where it stops being tight. That’s why the F4-424 Pro shipping with 32GB matters.

results.text:
Best Hardware for Unraid in 2026 | selfhosting.sh 
 Quick Recommendation
 Used Dell OptiPlex 5080 SFF ($150–$200) + Unraid Basic ($59). The i5-10500 handles Plex transcoding and Docker containers, you get 128 GB RAM max, and the SFF case fits two 3.5” drives plus an NVMe boot drive. Add a USB SATA dock for extra drives. Total build: ~$350 with 8 TB of storage.
 For a dedicated NAS build with 4+ drive bays, pair an Intel i3-12100 ($100) or i5-12400 ($130) with a Fractal Design Node 304 case ($80) and a motherboard with 4+ SATA ports. Total: ~$450 before drives.
 Get the Docker Compose configs, hardware picks, and setup shortcuts we don’t put in articles. Weekly. No spam.
 What Unraid Needs from Hardware
 Unraid is unique among NAS operating systems. Understanding its architecture tells you exactly what hardware to buy.
 How Unraid Storage Works
 Unraid doesn’t use traditional RAID. Instead:
 Each drive in the array is an independent filesystem (XFS or Btrfs)
 A parity drive protects against single-drive failure (or two failures with dual parity)
 Drives can be different sizes and brands — no matching required
 Only the drive being accessed spins up, saving power and wear
 This means:
 You don’t need a hardware RAID controller. In fact, don’t use one — Unraid manages drives directly via the motherboard’s SATA/HBA controller.
 SATA ports matter more than RAID support. Count the SATA ports on your motherboard. Each port = one array drive.
 The parity drive should be the largest drive. Equal to or larger than any data drive in the array.
 CPU Requirements
 Unraid itself is lightweight — it runs from a USB flash drive and barely touches the CPU. Your CPU choice depends on what you’ll run on top of Unraid:
 Use Case CPU Recommendation 
 NAS only (file serving) Any modern CPU — even an N100 works 
 NAS + Docker containers Intel i3/i5 or Ryzen 5 with QuickSync/AMF 
 NAS + Docker + Plex transcoding Intel i5+ with QuickSync (mandatory for HW transcode) 
 NAS + Docker + VMs Intel i5-12400+ or Ryzen 5 5600 (6+ cores) 
 NAS + Docker + VMs + GPU passthrough Intel i5-13500 or Ryzen 7 5700X with discrete GPU 
 Intel QuickSync is the deciding factor for Plex/Jellyfin users. AMD CPUs work fine for everything else, but Intel’s hardware transcoding is significantly better supported in media server containers on Unraid.
 For CPU details, see Best CPUs for Home Server and Intel vs AMD .
 RAM Requirements
 Workload Minimum Recommended 
 NAS only 4 GB 8 GB 
 NAS + Docker (5–10 containers) 8 GB 16 GB 
 NAS + Docker (15+ containers) 16 GB 32 GB 
 NAS + Docker + VMs 32 GB 64 GB 
 Unraid doesn’t require ECC RAM (unlike ZFS-based systems). Standard DDR4/DDR5 is fine. ECC works if your platform supports it but isn’t necessary.
 For RAM recommendations, see Best RAM for Home Server .
 Storage Controller
 Use the motherboard’s SATA ports for up to 4–6 drives. For more drives, add an HBA (Host Bus Adapter):
 Controller Ports Interface Price (Used) 
 LSI 9207-8i 8 SAS/SATA PCIe x8 $25–$40 
 Dell H310 (flashed to IT mode) 8 SAS/SATA PCIe x8 $15–$25 
 LSI 9211-8i 8 SAS/SATA PCIe x8 $20–$35 
 Broadcom 9500-8i 8 SAS/SATA PCIe x8 Gen4 $80–$120 
 Flash to IT mode. These cards often ship in RAID mode (IR firmware). Unraid needs direct disk access, which requires IT (Initiator Target) firmware. Search “flash LSI 9207-8i IT mode” for your specific card.
 SAS breakout cables ($10–$15 each) connect the SFF-8087 connector on the HBA to individual SATA drives. You need one cable per 4 drives.
 Boot Drive
 Unraid boots from a USB flash drive — not an SSD or HDD. The USB drive holds the Unraid OS and license key.
 Use a quality USB 2.0 or 3.0 flash drive. USB 2.0 is actually preferred — it’s more reliable for the constant small writes Unraid does. Recommended: SanDisk Ultra Fit 32 GB ($8).
 The cache drive (separate from the boot USB) is where Docker containers, VMs, and app data live. This should be a fast NVMe SSD:
 500 GB NVMe for Docker containers and VM images
 1 TB NVMe if you use the cache for writes before they move to the array
 Recommended: Samsung 970 EVO Plus 500 GB ($40) or WD Black SN770 500 GB ($35).

 Total ~$352

 Unraid-Specific Considerations
 Drive Sleep and Power
 Unraid only spins up drives that are being accessed. A 6-drive array with one active drive draws less power than a RAID array where all drives must spin together.
 Expect:
 Cache SSD + boot USB: 3–5W
 Each spinning 3.5” HDD: 6–8W active, 0.5W spun down
 System idle (CPU + board + 1 SSD): 15–30W depending on CPU
 A typical mid-range build with most drives spun down: 20–30W. All drives active: 50–70W.
 Parity Checks
 Unraid maintains parity in real-time — every write to the array updates the parity drive(s) immediately. Monthly parity checks verify this data by reading every drive to confirm consistency. These checks take 12–24 hours and all drives spin up simultaneously. Schedule them for a time when noise and power draw don’t matter (e.g., Tuesday 3 AM).
 Docker Storage: Cache vs Array
 Docker containers and their data should always live on the cache SSD, not the array. The array is slow (single-drive speed, not striped). Configuration:
 Set Docker image location to /mnt/cache/docker/ 
 Set Docker appdata to /mnt/cache/appdata/ 
 Set VM storage to /mnt/cache/vms/ 
 The array is for bulk data: media files, backups, documents.
 Community Applications (App Store)
 Install the Community Applications plugin — it’s Unraid’s app store. One-click installs for:
 Plex, Jellyfin, Emby
 Nextcloud, Vaultwarden, Home Assistant
 Pi-hole, AdGuard Home
 All the popular self-hosted apps
 Each app is a pre-configured Docker template. Easier than writing Docker Compose files manually.

 Plus 12 $89 Mid-range NAS with room to grow

 “Devices” includes all storage devices: array drives, parity drives, cache drives, and the boot USB. It does not count VMs or Docker containers.
 Recommendation: Buy Plus ($89). Six devices fills up fast once you add parity + cache + boot USB. The $30 difference between Basic and Plus is worth the headroom.
 FAQ
 Do I need ECC RAM for Unraid?
 No. Unraid’s main array uses XFS or Btrfs per-drive with parity protection — neither filesystem requires ECC the way ZFS does. Standard DDR4 is fine. Unraid 7.0+ added native ZFS support for cache pools, but even ZFS on Unraid works without ECC. ECC works if your platform supports it but isn’t required.
 Can I mix drive sizes?
 Yes — this is Unraid’s biggest advantage. The only rule: the parity drive must be equal to or larger than the largest data drive. So if you have 4 TB, 8 TB, and 12 TB data drives, your parity drive must be at least 12 TB.
 SSD array or HDD array?
 Unraid’s array is designed for HDDs — single-drive performance is fine for bulk storage. SSDs in the array are wasted because Unraid doesn’t stripe data across drives. Use SSDs for cache only. Use HDDs for the array.

For most buyers the best NAS under $500 is the QNAP TS-264 : dual 2.5GbE, two NVMe

 purchase, the drives must be CMR NAS-rated , never SMR, and RAID is not a
 backup .
 The one thing to know: RAID is not a backup. RAID (except RAID 0) protects against DRIVE failure — if one disk dies, the array keeps running while you replace it. It does nothing against the things that actually destroy data: accidental deletion, ransomware, file corruption, a failed controller, theft, fire, or a power surge that takes the whole box. All of those hit the live array and every mirror of it at once. RAID is about uptime and availability; a backup is a separate, ideally offline or off-site copy you can restore from. You need both, and 'I have RAID' is the single most common — and most dangerous — misconception in home storage.
 The under-$500 picks, ranked, with the honest drawback on each

 Every NAS above ships as an empty enclosure — the drives are the other half of the purchase. NAS-rated CMR drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf) are built for 24×7 duty, vibration in multi-bay chassis, and RAID rebuilds, which desktop drives are not.
 Best for: Anyone buying a NAS enclosure who needs reliable, rebuild-safe drives to populate it
 Our verdict: Whichever enclosure you choose, NAS-rated CMR drives are the right call — WD Red Plus and Seagate IronWolf are both proven lines built for 24×7 array duty, and either one belongs in your cart alongside the enclosure.

The plain WD Red (non-Plus) and many cheap desktop/external-shucked drives are SMR; confirm CMR on the spec sheet. Buy from a source with a clear return path in case of early failure, and always run a NAS with a real backup — RAID is not a backup.
 Complete your setup
 NAS-ready hard drives (CMR)
 Every enclosure above ships empty. Seagate IronWolf and WD Red Plus are the two proven NAS-rated CMR lines — confirm CMR on the spec sheet before you buy.

 UPS battery backup
 A NAS hates dirty shutdowns — a power cut mid-write can corrupt an array. A UPS in the APC Back-UPS line lets the NAS shut down cleanly when the lights go out.
Shop on Amazon →
 Cat6 Ethernet cable
 2.5GbE is only as good as the cable. Cat6 handles 2.5GbE (and 10GbE at short runs) — a cheap fix for a NAS still hanging off an old patch lead.
Shop on Amazon →
 What does under $500 actually buy?
 Three realities of the budget bracket that the bay-count marketing never mentions:
 The enclosure is half the bill
Every NAS here ships empty. NAS-rated CMR drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf) are bought
 separately and priced per drive by capacity, so the real budget is enclosure plus two or more
 drives. Size the drives for the data you will have in three years, not the data you have today.
 2-bay mirror math, or 4-bay (n-1) math
A 2-bay in RAID 1 gives you ONE drive's worth of usable space: 2×8TB = 8TB. A 4-bay in RAID 5 or
 single-redundancy SHR gives up only one drive: 4×8TB ≈ 24TB usable, with one-at-a-time upgrades
 instead of the 2-bay's both-drives upgrade trap. At this bracket the F4-424 is the 4-bay that fits.
 How many bays do you really need? → 
 Hardware value or software polish, not both
Synology sells software polish on older, slower hardware (a 2020-era Celeron, 2GB base RAM, no NVMe
 on the DS225+). QNAP, TerraMaster and UGREEN sell current hardware (2.5GbE, NVMe, 8GB) with software that
 is either busier (QTS), less mature (TOS) or younger (UGOS Pro). Decide which you are paying for.
 The spec that splits this bracket: 2.5GbE vs 1GbE
 2.5GbE matters because 1GbE is the real bottleneck in most NAS setups. A 1GbE link tops out around 110–118MB/s of actual throughput — and a single modern hard drive already reads at roughly 180–280MB/s sequentially, so on gigabit you're leaving half the drive's speed on the table, and a RAID array or NVMe cache is throttled even harder. 2.5GbE lifts the ceiling to ~280MB/s, roughly matching one fast HDD and dramatically improving large-file transfers. It's the single most worthwhile 'speed' upgrade for home NAS; 10GbE only pays off with NVMe pools or many-drive arrays. All four picks now ship 2.5GbE: the TS-264 and F4-424 with two ports, the
 DXP2800 and the Synology DS225+ with one (the DS225+ pairs it with a 1GbE port; its predecessor, the
 DS224+, was 1GbE only).

 How do the four compare on the specs that decide it?
From our master spec data: CPU class, RAM ceiling, networking, NVMe, operating system and whether the
 chip can hardware-transcode. None of these four has ECC; that is a feature of the prosumer tier below.

 What you give up versus the tier above
Just above this bracket, the Synology DS425+ buys DSM at four bays: the same J4125
 and 6GB RAM ceiling as the DS225+, plus two M.2 slots for SSD cache. Synology's ECC 4-bay, the
 DS925+ , is what more money buys: ECC memory expandable to 32GB and two 2.5GbE ports, but
 no integrated GPU, so it is a poor Plex transcoding box, which is exactly the job many budget buyers want
 done. The mid-tier 4-bays, the QNAP TS-464 
(PCIe Gen3 slot for a 10GbE card later) and the UGREEN DXP4800 (dual 2.5GbE, four bays
 plus two M.2), and the Asustor AS5404T with its four M.2 slots, sit between the two.
 If the budget stretches, start with best 4-bay NAS ; if the question is
 whether you need ECC at all, read ECC is nice, not mandatory first.
 Which drives belong in a budget NAS?
 NAS-rated drives use CMR (conventional magnetic recording); many cheap desktop and external drives use SMR (shingled), which overlaps tracks to pack in more capacity but must rewrite whole zones on write, making sustained and random writes slow. In a NAS this matters most during a RAID rebuild: an SMR drive can slow a rebuild to a crawl or cause it to drop out of the array, risking a second failure before it finishes. Use CMR NAS drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf) in an array; the plain WD Red was infamously SMR. Always confirm CMR on the spec sheet. The temptation at this bracket is to save on drives after spending on the
 enclosure. Do not: a rebuild after a failure is your single window of vulnerability, and an SMR drive
 stretching that window is exactly the risk you bought RAID to avoid.
 CMR vs SMR, decoded →

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS under $500? ▼ For most buyers it is the QNAP TS-264: a 2-bay with dual 2.5GbE, two M.2 NVMe slots and 8GB of RAM out of the box, which is more hardware than any rival at its tier. If you want four bays in the same money, the TerraMaster F4-424 is the raw hardware-value pick (Intel N95, 8GB DDR5 expandable to 32GB, dual 2.5GbE) and openly supports TrueNAS or Unraid. If you want the most polished software and the least tinkering, the Synology DS225+ is the turnkey box, at the cost of 2GB base RAM (6GB maximum), one 2.5GbE port and no NVMe. All of these are enclosure prices only: the drives are a separate purchase, and prices move, so confirm the bracket on the live listing.
 Does 'under $500' include the drives? ▼ No. Every NAS on this page ships as an empty enclosure, and the drives are the other half of the purchase, priced per drive by capacity. Budget for NAS-rated CMR drives (WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf) on top of the enclosure. Avoid SMR (shingled) drives in a RAID array: their slow rewrite behavior can make a rebuild crawl or fail, and the plain WD Red (non-Plus) and many cheap desktop or shucked drives are SMR. Confirm CMR on the spec sheet.
 2-bay or 4-bay at this budget? ▼ A 2-bay mirror (RAID 1) gives you one drive's worth of usable space (2×8TB = 8TB) and covers most homes: photos, documents, PC backups and a light media library. A 4-bay in RAID 5 or single-redundancy SHR gives you roughly (n-1) drives of usable space (4×8TB ≈ 24TB) plus one-at-a-time capacity upgrades and an escape hatch to two-drive redundancy. At this bracket the TerraMaster F4-424 is the 4-bay that fits; a 4-bay running only two drives at first is often the smarter buy because it keeps a growth path a 2-bay can never offer.
 Which budget NAS is best for Plex or Jellyfin? ▼ All four picks have Intel CPUs with integrated graphics that handle hardware transcoding: the QNAP TS-264 (N5105), TerraMaster F4-424 (N95), UGREEN DXP2800 (N100) and Synology DS225+ (J4125, H.264/H.265). The TS-264, F4-424 and DXP2800 have the edge for a media-heavy setup because of newer CPUs, more RAM and NVMe slots; the DS225+'s 2GB base RAM (6GB maximum) makes it the weakest of the four for that job.
 Is the Synology DS225+ worth it over the cheaper-hardware brands? ▼ It is if the appliance experience is what you are buying. DSM is the most polished, best-documented NAS operating system, with the widest first-party app ecosystem, and the DS225+ is the lowest-friction way into NAS. What you give up is hardware: a 2020-era Celeron J4125, 2GB base RAM (6GB maximum), one 2.5GbE port rather than two, and no NVMe. QNAP, TerraMaster and UGREEN sell current hardware (2.5GbE, NVMe, 8GB) with software that is either busier (QTS), less mature (TOS) or younger (UGOS Pro).
 Is RAID on a budget NAS a backup? ▼ No. RAID (except RAID 0) protects against one drive failing, keeping the array online while you replace the disk. It does nothing against accidental deletion, ransomware, corruption, theft, fire or a power surge, all of which hit the live array and every mirror at once. Treat the NAS as one copy in a 3-2-1 scheme: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site. A budget NAS plus a cloud or off-site copy is a real setup; a NAS alone is not.
 How we work
We're a research-based site: we analyze manufacturer specifications, storage and filesystem engineering,
 and aggregated owner-feedback themes rather than lab-testing every enclosure. We explain tradeoffs plainly,
 always name a downside, and report measurable specs, never a guarantee about data safety. RAID is not a
 backup, drives fail, and only a tested 3-2-1 backup protects your data.
